ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is a clonal stem‑cell disorder causing complement‑mediated red cell lysis, thrombosis, and bone‑marrow failure. It presents with hemoglobinuria, anemia, and venous clots.

sections.p: PNH is a somatic mutation in the PIG-A gene, leading to loss of GPI‑anchored proteins that protect cells from complement. Diagnosis requires flow cytometry for CD55/59 deficiency and confirmation of the PIG‑A mutation.

t.b: Detects complement regulatory protein loss; positive result confirms PNH
Shows schistocytes and hemoglobinuria; supports hemolysis
Usually normal; low C3 may indicate consumption

sections.p: The revised International PNH Classification grades disease by hemolysis, marrow failure, and thrombosis. Stages range from mild hemolysis (stage I) to severe marrow failure with pancytopenia (stage IV).
The primary cause is a somatic mutation in the PIG‑A gene in hematopoietic stem cells. Secondary triggers include infections, autoimmune disease, and malignancy.
Patients often report dark urine after waking, fatigue, dyspnea, abdominal pain, and swelling. Recurrent venous thrombosis, especially hepatic or portal veins, is common.
Key tests confirm hemolysis, rule out other causes, and assess complications. In low‑resource settings, basic labs and a simple flow cytometry panel are essential.
Urgent care is needed for sudden severe anemia, massive hemoglobinuria, or unexplained thrombosis. Long‑term risks include pulmonary hypertension and acute leukemia.
Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and prevent thrombosis. Eculizumab or ravulizumab blocks complement C5, reducing hemolysis. Anticoagulation is used for thrombosis.
b: Complement inhibition (eculizumab/ravulizumab) – reduces hemolysis and thrombosis

t.b: Blocks C5; prevents MAC formation; reduces hemolysis
Prevents venous thrombosis; monitor INR or drug levels

sections.p: Regular monitoring of hemoglobin, LDH, and flow cytometry is essential. Vaccination against meningococci is mandatory before complement inhibitors. Early detection of thrombosis improves outcomes.
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, sickle cell crisis, and thrombotic microangiopathies can mimic PNH.
Low LDH or normal reticulocyte count can occur in chronic disease; a negative Coombs test may be falsely positive if complement is low. Flow cytometry requires fresh samples.
b: False negative Coombs if complement low

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe anemia with dark urine

faq.q: Why does PNH cause hemoglobinuria at night?
faq.a: During sleep, blood pressure falls and plasma volume decreases, increasing complement activation and red cell lysis.
No, but complement inhibitors control hemolysis and reduce complications; bone marrow transplant is the only curative option.

faq.q: What is the role of flow cytometry?
faq.a: It detects missing GPI‑anchored proteins on blood cells, confirming the diagnosis.
